topic.title: Fantasy apps changed who we cheer for
topic.claim: Fantasy cricket quietly turned fans of teams into fans of their own points, and a six against your team can now make you happy.
topic.moment: Your team is losing, but you cheer because the opposition batter is your captain.

turn.believed: We watch cricket for our team.
turn.actually: Many of us now watch for our fantasy squad, and loyalty got split across both sides.

topic.because: Fantasy apps make money when every ball matters to you personally. Team loyalty doesn't pay them, your players do.
topic.payoff: Test: did you cheer for the other team's wicket-keeper this season?
topic.behaviour: Fans track player points and cheer for individuals across teams.
topic.mechanism: Money on players breaks loyalty to teams.
topic.send_to: The friend who celebrated a wicket against their own city's team.
topic.why_now: The cricket season is busy, and fantasy talk fills every group chat.

score.why: Fantasy apps split fan loyalty, so a six against your team can make you happy. Funny and true.

cover.headline: Fantasy cricket turned you into a fan of [your own points]
cover.sub: Your loyalty now sits on both sides of every ball.

paragraphs: Fantasy cricket turned you into a fan of your own points.
slides.why_swipe: How does a six against your own team make you happy?

paragraphs: It's a weekend match. The toss is done, the lineups are out, and you have a few minutes to fix your team before it locks.
You make the other side's opener captain. He scores big at this ground, so the choice takes two seconds. Their wicket-keeper goes in too, for the catches.
slides.why_swipe: What happens when that opener walks out against your team?

paragraphs: Your team needs early wickets. He drives the second ball over long-on for six. The room groans, and you groan with it.
Your face looks as sad as everyone's while your thumb is already opening the app. Points up. **You hide the small smile from the room.**
slides.why_swipe: So what do you actually feel when the match ends?

paragraphs: Your team loses by a big margin. In bed, you replay one thing, and it isn't the result. It's your captain's run-out in the 15th over.
The group chat skips the scorecard. Just rank screenshots, and everyone roasting that run-out. "Bhai, captain ne hi dooba diya."
slides.why_swipe: Why does the run-out sting more than the loss?

paragraphs: A ball only matters to the app if it matters to you personally. Your team's colours don't pay it. Your eleven does.
And yes, that has a good side. The last ten overs of a one-sided match used to be when you checked your phone. Now you watch every ball.
The cost is that you watch it with your loyalty split across both sides.
slides.why_swipe: So which side are you really on?

paragraphs: The other side's wicket-keeper, the one you picked for catches, hits a fifty against your team. Your hands clap before you've thought about it.
**Count whose fifties you clapped for this season. Then check whose side you were on.**

end.save: Come back to it after your next late-night leaderboard check.
end.send: The friend who celebrated a wicket against their own city's team.
end.promise: Why we watch what we watch.

draft.caption: Which player from the other team have you secretly cheered for this season, and what did it cost your own side?
draft.alt_text: A six-slide carousel arguing that fantasy cricket has split fans' loyalty between their team and their fantasy squad. It follows a reader who makes an opposition opener their captain because he scores big at that ground, and picks the opposition wicket-keeper for catches. The reader groans with the room when the opener hits a six against their own team while their phone shows points going up. After a heavy loss they replay the captain's run-out instead of the result, while the group chat roasts the run-out and shares rank screenshots. It explains that a ball only matters to the app if it matters to you personally, so your eleven pays it and your team's colours don't. It admits this makes the dead overs of a one-sided match worth watching, but leaves your loyalty split. It ends with a test: count whose fifties you clapped for this season, then check whose side you were on.
